questions.q: Why is dw.FactWorkOrder classified as an accumulating snapshot fact table rather than a plain transaction fact?
options: A work order has a defined lifecycle — started, due, and eventually ended — so the fact row is inserted at the start and updated as StockedQty/ScrappedQty change and EndDateKey is filled in, rather than inserted once and left alone
It's classified this way purely because it has more than three columns
Because it never gets updated after the initial insert
Because it aggregates data on a fixed schedule, like once per day
questions.explain: The insert-then-update-until-complete lifecycle is exactly what distinguishes an accumulating snapshot from a transaction fact (insert-only) or a periodic snapshot (scheduled batch inserts).

questions.q: Why do StartDateKey, EndDateKey, and DueDateKey all reference the same physical dw.DimDate table instead of three separate date dimensions?
options: This is a role-playing dimension — one physical table serving three distinct business roles avoids three separate ETL loads and the risk of the same calendar date looking different across duplicated copies
SQL Server does not allow more than one date dimension per database
The three dates are always identical, so only one lookup is needed
It's a performance optimization with no relationship to dimensional modeling concepts
questions.explain: Same mechanism as Data Modeling & Data Warehousing's Lesson 27 — one physical dimension, multiple foreign keys, each a distinct role.

questions.q: Why is EndDateKey nullable on dw.FactWorkOrder while StartDateKey and DueDateKey are not?
options: A work order that hasn't finished yet has no end date — the row is inserted when the work order starts, before it has ended, and EndDateKey gets filled in once it completes
EndDateKey is nullable because it's never actually used
StartDateKey and DueDateKey are always the same value, so only one needs to be required
SQL Server requires the last column in a CREATE TABLE statement to be nullable
questions.explain: This nullability is a direct consequence of the accumulating snapshot load pattern — the row exists before the work order is done.

questions.q: Why isn't Production.Location modeled as a dimension on dw.FactWorkOrder, even though it's a real, related AdventureWorks2012 table?
options: Location is tracked at the WorkOrderRouting (operation) grain, one level finer than the WorkOrder grain this fact table chose — attaching one LocationKey per work order would silently pick just one location for a work order that may have touched several
Production.Location doesn't actually exist in AdventureWorks2012
Location data is already fully captured by DimProduct
Adding a fourth dimension would exceed SQL Server's column limit
questions.explain: This is a genuine grain mismatch, not a simplification — modeling it correctly would require a separate fact table at the routing grain or a many-to-many bridge, both out of scope for this capstone.

questions.q: Which group does WorkOrderID belong to on dw.FactWorkOrder, and why?
options: A degenerate dimension — it identifies the work order itself and isn't worth a separate one-column dimension table
A measure — it gets summed in reports
A role-playing foreign key to DimDate
A surrogate key resolved by a Lookup transformation
questions.explain: WorkOrderID rides directly on the fact row as a degenerate dimension, the same pattern Data Modeling & Data Warehousing's capstone used for PurchaseOrderID.
